indefinite_article.definition: Used before nouns to indicate a single, nonspecific item or individual.
indefinite_article.example: She found a book on the table.
indefinite_article.usage_notes: Used before consonant sounds; 'an' is used before vowel sounds.

indefinite_article.definition: Used to introduce someone or something for the first time.
indefinite_article.example: There was a loud noise outside.
indefinite_article.usage_notes: Often used in storytelling or descriptions.

indefinite_article.definition: Used to express a rate or ratio.
indefinite_article.example: He earns fifty dollars a day.

indefinite_article.definition: Used before a singular noun to represent an entire class or kind.
indefinite_article.example: A dog is a loyal animal.

indefinite_article.definition: Used before a person's name to indicate someone unknown to the speaker.
indefinite_article.example: A Mr. Smith called for you.
indefinite_article.usage_notes: Often implies the speaker does not know the person well.

usage_notes.general: The indefinite article 'a' is one of the most commonly used words in English. It is used before singular, countable nouns that begin with consonant sounds.

regional_variations.UK: Pronunciation may sometimes lean towards 'ə' in casual speech.
regional_variations.US: Pronunciation is typically 'ā' in most contexts.

usage_notes.special_cases: Before words starting with a vowel sound, 'an' is used instead (e.g., 'an apple').

adjective.definition: Having the power, skill, means, or opportunity to do something.
adjective.example: She was able to finish the project on time.
adjective.usage_notes: Often followed by an infinitive verb ('to' + base verb).

adjective.definition: Having considerable skill, proficiency, or intelligence.
adjective.example: He is an able lawyer who wins most of his cases.
adjective.usage_notes: Used to describe someone highly skilled in a particular area.

etymology: Middle English: from Old French, from Latin habilis 'handy, skillful', from habere 'to hold'.

usage_notes.general: The word 'able' is commonly used to describe capability or skill. It is often paired with 'to' + verb to indicate capacity.

preposition.definition: In or to a higher place than; over.
preposition.example: The bird flew above the trees.

preposition.definition: Higher in rank, status, or importance than.
preposition.example: A captain is above a lieutenant in rank.

adverb.definition: In or to a higher place; overhead.
Higher on the same page or on a preceding page.
adverb.example: As stated above, the results were inconclusive.

adjective.definition: Mentioned or appearing earlier in the same text.
adjective.example: Refer to the above diagram for clarification.

noun.definition: Something that is above or overhead.
noun.example: The above is a photograph of the building.

etymology: Old English abufan, onbufan, from a- 'on' + bufan 'above' (from bi 'by' + ufan 'above').

usage_notes.general: 'Above' is a versatile word used in spatial, hierarchical, and textual contexts.

adjective.definition: Not qualified or diminished in any way; total.
adjective.example: She had absolute trust in her lawyer.

adjective.definition: Viewed or existing independently and not in relation to other things; not relative or comparative.
adjective.example: Absolute moral standards must guide our decisions.
adjective.usage_notes: Common in philosophical or ethical contexts.

adjective.definition: Free from imperfection; perfect or complete.
adjective.example: The artist sought absolute beauty in his work.
adjective.usage_notes: Often used in aesthetic or ideal contexts.

adjective.definition: Not limited by restrictions or exceptions; unconditional.
adjective.usage_notes: Frequently used in political or authoritative contexts.

noun.definition: A value or principle that is regarded as universally valid or may be viewed without relation to other things.
noun.example: Some philosophers argue that good and evil are absolutes.
noun.usage_notes: Common in philosophical or theoretical discussions.

noun.definition: A substance that is free from impurities or adulterants.
noun.example: The chemist isolated the absolute from the compound.
noun.usage_notes: Technical term in chemistry or perfumery.

etymology: Late Middle English: from Latin absolutus 'freed, unrestricted', past participle of absolvere (see absolve).

usage_notes.general: The word 'absolute' is versatile, used in contexts ranging from philosophy to everyday emphasis.

regional_variations.UK: Sometimes pronounced with a stronger emphasis on the second syllable.
regional_variations.US: More commonly pronounced with primary stress on the first syllable.

preposition.example: She told me about her trip to Japan.
preposition.usage_notes: Commonly used to introduce topics in conversation or writing.

preposition.definition: In the vicinity of; near to.
preposition.example: He lives about five miles from here.
preposition.usage_notes: Often used to give approximate locations or distances.
